opening.argument: The video pairs attractive income figures with a concrete viewer action: it highlights developer earnings up to $85,000 annually and directs viewers to an external salary calculator. That turns career information into a solicitation to follow the linked path and enter personal role, location, education, experience, and technology details in pursuit of a higher salary estimate. The viewer is not merely shown general education; the promised financial outcome is placed alongside a tool and an invitation to use it. Because the figures are presented as what viewers can earn, the combination can function as a low-friction income-acquisition pitch even though the video does not spell out a payment step.

opening.argument: Several risk signals are concentrated in a short presentation: prominent salary amounts, an external calculator URL, and a direct invitation to check the tool. The headline itself promises the “highest salary” jobs, while the video reduces a complicated employment market to a ranked list of annual figures. Viewers are encouraged to compare themselves against those numbers through an outside site, yet the figures are limited to a 2019 survey and do not establish that any particular viewer will obtain them. That combination of large income claims, external redirection, and simplified access can reasonably appear deceptive rather than a neutral warning.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats each signal in isolation. The relevant pattern is the emphatic “highest salary” framing, specific dollar figures, and an external calculator presented as the next step. Even if the source is named, that does not verify that the ranking applies to the viewer or that the calculator produces a reliable result. The presentation creates confidence before establishing those limitations.

The surrounding call to subscribe and follow the channel reinforces an acquisition funnel: first attract viewers with income, then direct them to an external tool and future content.
